questions.q: What is the 'leverage effect' observed in equity markets?
options: Volatility is always higher on days with high trading volume
Negative return shocks tend to raise future volatility more than positive shocks of the same magnitude
Stock prices with more financial leverage always have lower volatility
Interest rate changes have no effect on equity volatility
questions.explain: The leverage effect describes the empirical pattern where negative shocks (bad news) increase future volatility by more than equally sized positive shocks (good news) — an asymmetry plain GARCH cannot represent.

questions.q: Why can't a standard GARCH(1,1) model capture the leverage effect?
options: GARCH(1,1) does not use any past shocks at all
The term eps_(t-1)^2 is identical regardless of whether the shock was positive or negative, so the model cannot distinguish the two
GARCH(1,1) only works on monthly data
GARCH(1,1) requires alpha + beta > 1
questions.explain: Because standard GARCH only enters the lagged shock as its square, a negative and a positive shock of the same magnitude produce exactly the same contribution to next period's variance — the model has no way to react differently to the sign.

questions.q: In a GJR-GARCH model, what does the indicator term gamma*I_(t-1)*eps_(t-1)^2 do?
options: It subtracts variance whenever the previous shock was positive
It adds extra variance specifically when the previous shock was negative, if gamma is positive
It forces the model to ignore all shocks beyond lag 1
It replaces the omega constant entirely
questions.explain: I_(t-1) equals 1 only when the prior shock was negative, so a positive gamma adds an extra gamma*eps_(t-1)^2 contribution to variance specifically after negative shocks, directly modeling the leverage effect.

questions.q: What is a key structural advantage of EGARCH's log-variance formulation compared to standard GARCH?
options: It requires fewer total parameters than GARCH(1,1)
It guarantees conditional variance stays positive without needing explicit non-negativity constraints on the parameters
It eliminates the need for maximum likelihood estimation
It can only be fit on monthly, not daily, data
questions.explain: Because EGARCH models log(sigma_t^2) rather than sigma_t^2 directly, exponentiating the result always yields a positive variance, removing the need for the non-negativity constraints that plain GARCH and ARCH require on their coefficients.

questions.q: In the arch package, how do you specify a GJR-GARCH(1,1) model instead of plain GARCH(1,1)?
options: arch_model(returns, vol='GARCH', p=1, q=1)
arch_model(returns, vol='GARCH', p=1, o=1, q=1)
ARIMA(returns, order=(1,1,1))
VAR(returns).fit(1)
questions.explain: Adding o=1 to a standard GARCH specification in the arch package adds the GJR asymmetry (leverage) term on top of the usual GARCH(p, q) structure.
